title: Does the op-ed effect hold for respondents who oppose spending?
rationale: The source op-ed effect on support was 0.638 overall, but the pro-spending effect was 0.657 (n = 380) while the anti-spending effect was 0.232 (SE 0.454, n = 59). The treatment-by-group interaction of 0.425 (SE 0.476, p = 0.372) is inconclusive because the anti group was so small. A balanced sample can estimate both effects and their difference.
contribution: Estimates the op-ed effect separately for anti- and pro-spending respondents in a sample balanced by design, and tests the interaction directly.
limitations: Screening may change how respondents answer the later position question (consistency pressure).
Placebo arm still includes a chatbot, so this estimates the op-ed effect, not the chatbot effect.
Interaction power is lower than power for the within-group effects.

design.title: Op-ed effect by prior position on infrastructure spending
design.overview: Respondents are screened for their position on infrastructure spending. Equal numbers of pro- and anti-spending respondents are recruited. Within each group they are randomised to an op-ed against their own position or an unrelated placebo article. Everyone then chats with a chatbot and answers support and certainty items.
design.hypothesis: The op-ed raises support toward the op-ed position in both groups. The effect for anti-spending respondents is smaller than for pro-spending respondents (positive pro-by-treatment interaction).
design.primaryOutcome: Support moved toward the op-ed position (1-7, recoded so higher = closer to the op-ed position).
design.comparison: Op-ed + chatbot versus placebo + chatbot, within pro and anti groups, and the treatment-by-group interaction.
design.population: US adults on an online panel, pre-screened on infrastructure spending position; about 600 pro and 600 anti-spending respondents.

conditions.title: Op-ed + chatbot
conditions.description: Op-ed against the respondent's own position, then chatbot conversation.

conditions.title: Placebo + chatbot
conditions.description: Unrelated placebo article, then chatbot conversation.

questions.text: This is a research study about opinions and a chatbot conversation. It takes about 10 minutes and is voluntary. Do you agree to participate?
Do you support or oppose increased government spending on infrastructure?
Please read the following op-ed, which argues against your own position on infrastructure spending, and then continue. {{ed:article}}
Please read the following article and then continue. {{ed:article}}
Next you will talk with a chatbot about infrastructure spending and the article you read. Please discuss for a few exchanges.
How much do you support increased government spending on infrastructure? (1 = strongly oppose, 7 = strongly support)
How certain are you of your position on infrastructure spending? (0 = not at all, 100 = completely)
Thank you. The op-ed and article were written for research. The chatbot is an automated program. Your answers are confidential.

assumptions: About 300 per cell (about 1,200 total, 600 per group) gives 80% power to detect 0.32 at the source H1 SD of 1.49; detecting the interaction of 0.425 needs more.
The anti-spending effect observed was 0.232 (SE 0.454, n = 59), so the pro-spending 0.657 is the reference.
Equal pro and anti recruitment by pre-screening a large CloudResearch panel; randomisation within group.
Outcome recoding: 8-strength for pro, strength for anti, as in the source.
Compensation at standard panel rates for 10 minutes.
unresolved: The op-ed texts (against pro and against anti positions), placebo article and chatbot configuration must be supplied by the research team.
IRB approval number and compensation amount.
